what_it_does: Modern processors speed up execution by running instructions ahead of time based on guesses about what will happen next — a technique called speculative or transient execution. Attacks like Spectre and Meltdown exploit this: while the processor is speculatively executing code that will later be cancelled, it can briefly touch secret data, leaving faint traces in the cache (the fast on-chip memory) that an attacker can measure. Finding new variants of these bugs automatically is very hard because you need to get the processor's internal microarchitectural state (which cache lines are loaded, which branch predictor entries are primed) set up in exactly the right way. DejaVuzz is a hardware fuzzer — a tool that bombards a processor with random test programs to hunt for bugs — that solves both problems. Its first innovation, Dynamic Swappable Memory (DSM), can swap the physical memory behind a virtual address at runtime, precisely resetting the processor's internal caches and tables between tests so each test starts from a known state. Its second innovation, Differential Information Flow Tracking (DIFT), instruments a processor simulator to watch whether data tagged as secret ever reaches a place (such as a cache timing difference) that an attacker outside the secure zone could observe. Together, DSM and DIFT let DejaVuzz reliably trigger speculative execution windows and unambiguously detect whether secret data leaks as a result.
